topics.title: SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission
bullets: A high-powered US nuclear ‘executive mission’ will visit India from May 17–21, 2026 to assess the country’s nuclear energy landscape and identify cooperation opportunities following the passage of the SHANTI Act (2025) .
The mission is organized by the Washington DC-based Nuclear Energy Institute (a lobby group of America’s commercial nuclear industry) and the US India Strategic Partnership Forum (USISPF).

It will meet with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, Power Minister Manohar Lal, and Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat, and will also hold sessions with the private sector in Mumbai. What is Shanti Act? –
The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025, was passed by Parliament in December 2025 .
It repeals and replaces the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, consolidating India’s nuclear legal framework into a single, modern statute.
It is designed to re-engineer India’s nuclear sector from a state monopoly to a regulated, multi-player market.
The 1962 Atomic Energy Act was drafted for an era of autarky and kept nuclear power generation the exclusive preserve of the government (primarily NPCIL).
The 2010 Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act created a right of operator recourse against suppliers, which foreign companies found too risky and deterred investment.
Over six decades, this framework restricted nuclear power to less than 3% of India’s electricity mix, with nuclear contributing only 3.1% in 2024-25 and installed capacity of just 8.78 GW.

The new Act explicitly permits private Indian companies to build, own and operate nuclear power plants, fabricate nuclear fuel, and import/export nuclear fuel – breaking the decades-long state monopoly.
Instead of a uniform ₹1,500 crore cap, the Act introduces graded operator liability based on reactor size, ranging from ₹100 crore to ₹3,000 crore.

The right of recourse against suppliers is no longer statutory; it is now governed by the contract between operator and supplier, which makes India’s liability regime more predictable for global vendors.
The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) gets statutory status – it no longer functions merely through an executive order, enhancing its authority and independence.
The government retains tight control over fissile materials, spent fuel and heavy water, and private entities cannot manage sensitive materials .
A multi-layered compensation mechanism includes the liability cap, a government-backed Nuclear Liability Fund, and India’s participation in the Convention on Supplementary Compensation.
The government’s stated rationale is to provide clean, firm (24×7) baseload power that complements renewable energy, which is intermittent.
The target requires scaling up construction from the current small reactor programme (220-700 MW) to a fleet-level roll-out, which private capital is expected to accelerate.

SHANTI places a special emphasis on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) as a next-generation technology that is simpler to finance and deploy in smaller grids. India aims to commission indigenous SMRs by 2033,
The US-India Agreement for Nuclear Cooperation (commonly called the 123 Agreement) was signed in October 2008, enabling India to access nuclear exports from the US.
Implementation was held up for years because of India’s liability regime (the 2010 Act).

With SHANTI removing the statutory recourse-against-suppliers' clause, the 123 Agreement can now be operationalized, paving the way for projects using Light Water Reactors (LWRs) that dominate global nuclear commerce.
On 29 March 2026, India and the US completed negotiations on a reprocessing agreement that grants India the right to reprocess US-origin spent nuclear fuel at a dedicated national facility.
This separate arrangement, envisaged in the 123 Agreement, gives India the same ability to close the fuel cycle that was previously enjoyed only by countries like Japan and Euratom.
Completion of this reprocessing protocol removes a final non-proliferation hurdle and is expected to clear the way for US reactor vendors to bid for projects in India. Nuclear Fleet of India –
India operates 25 nuclear power reactors with a total capacity of 8,800 MW.
The fleet is spread across eight power stations in Tamil Nadu (Kudankulam, MAPS), Maharashtra (Tarapur), Rajasthan (RAPS), Karnataka (Kaiga), Gujarat (Kakrapar), and Uttar Pradesh (Narora).
The largest operational reactors are two VVER units at Kudankulam (2,000 MW), followed by four PHWR units at Kakrapar (1,840 MW) and four at Tarapur (1,400 MW).
Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS) Unit-7 (700 MW) achieved full-power commercial operation on April 15, 2025, becoming India's newest operational large reactor.
It is part of a batch of sixteen indigenous 700 MW Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors being built across the country to expand nuclear capacity.
Its twin unit RAPP-8 is expected soon, and GHAVP-1 & 2 at Gorakhpur (Haryana) are also under construction.
17 nuclear power reactors with a total capacity of 13,100 MW are under implementation, including 7 under physical construction and 10 under pre-project activities.
Major reactors under construction include Kudankulam Units 3 & 4 (2 x 1,000 MW) in Tamil Nadu and two indigenous 700 MW PHWRs at Kaiga in Karnataka.
At Kudankulam, fuel loading for Unit-3 began in early 2025, and the unit reached a key commissioning milestone in April 2026.
Construction of two new 700 MW PHWRs (Kaiga Units 5 and 6) was approved and officially commenced in February 2026.
NPCIL awarded the first major civilian contract (nearly ₹12,000 crore) to a consortium led by Megha Engineering & Infrastructure Ltd to build these reactors.
The project is expected to be completed by 2030-31, significantly boosting nuclear capacity in Southern India.
The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) granted a major permit on April 30, 2026, allowing NPCIL to erect major equipment at Kudankulam Units 5 and 6.
The permit covers key components like Reactor Pressure Vessel, Steam Generators, and Coolant Pumps for the Russian-designed VVER-1000 reactors.
This decision transitioned the project from civil construction to the critical plant installation phase, accelerating progress.
The SHANTI Act establishes a dedicated Nuclear Liability Fund to compensate victims in case of a nuclear incident, stepping in when damages exceed the operator's liability cap.
The Nuclear Energy Mission, announced in the Union Budget 2025-26, provides dedicated policy and financial push to nuclear power.
A total provision of ₹20,000 crore has been made for R&D, design, and deployment of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) under this mission.
Installed nuclear capacity, which was just 4,780 MW in 2014, has increased to 8,780 MW (an 84% rise) and is projected to reach nearly 22,380 MW by 2031-32.
The ambitious roadmap beyond 2032 targets: 47 GW by 2037, 67 GW by 2042, and 100 GW by 2047, 12-fold increase from current levels.
This growth will be driven by completion of large PHWRs, VVERs under construction, and a new generation of SMRs.
India's 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, achieved first criticality on April 6, 2026.
This milestone makes India only the second country in the world after Russia to operate a commercial-scale Fast Breeder Reactor.
The PFBR launches India's second stage of the three-stage nuclear programme, enabling utilisation of thorium reserves for future power generation.

India is actively developing three distinct types of SMRs: the 220 MWe Bharat SMR (BSMR-200) , the 55 MWe SMR-55, and an up to 5 MWth High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactor (HTGR) for hydrogen generation.
The BSMR-200 and SMR-55 are designed to repurpose retiring coal plant sites, while the HTGR is for industrial heat and hydrogen.
A site for the lead BSMR-200 unit has been proposed at Tarapur, Maharashtra.
Section 3(e) of the SHANTI Act allows ‘any other person’ permitted by the Central Government through notification, hinting at foreign participation without explicitly mentioning FDI.
Building on the SHANTI Act, the government will soon invite bids for a 220 MWe Bharat SMR (BSMR-200), marking a key milestone for private participation in the nuclear sector.
This would be the first time a private Indian company enters the operations side of India's nuclear power programme. Recent News –
The US delegation is led by the Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI), the trade association that represents all US nuclear reactor manufacturers and fuel suppliers.
It is co-organized with the US India Strategic Partnership Forum (USISPF), a powerful advocacy group that has worked for years to remove India’s liability barriers.
The mission is explicitly designed to “take stock of India’s nuclear landscape” after SHANTI and to coordinate US industry messaging on the new opportunities.

The delegation lands in New Delhi on 17 May and stays there until 19 May, holding meetings with the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), NPCIL, NITI Aayog, other energy ministries and central ministers.
On 20–21 May, the team moves to Mumbai to meet private sector giants: Reliance, Adani Group, Tata Power, JSW Energy, Vedanta, L&T, Tata Consulting Engineers and Hindalco.
US Ambassador Sergio Gor and the US Embassy will set the agenda for the formal meetings, which start on the morning of 18 May in Delhi.

One of the most significant features of the mission is the Mumbai leg, where the US team will meet more than eight major Indian private corporate groups that are not part of the traditional public-sector nuclear ecosystem.
This will mark the first major interface between the US industry and India’s private sector after the enactment of SHANTI.
In April 2026, the US and India announced a separate agreement to build six large US nuclear power plants in India, giving a concrete shape to the revived cooperation.

At the same time, India has also been deepening its strategic nuclear partnership with Russia: a fresh procurement of five additional S-400 units has been cleared, and work on Unit 3 & 4 of the Kudankulam project (Russian-designed VVER reactors) is progressing.

The government has clearly stated that the technology will be the main criterion ─ not the nationality of the supplier ─ as long as the liability and safety conditions are met. The proposed legislation aimed to address issues related to redistribution of parliamentary seats and constituency boundaries based on demographic changes. Delimitation refers to the process of redrawing the boundaries of electoral constituencies to reflect population changes recorded through the Census.
